passage: The auto slowed at the big junction near the vegetable market, and Pooja's hand went to the seat rail, the way it had every day since the scooter crash last winter. This time she counted the flower stalls instead: one, two, three heaps of marigolds. Her routine held her up: chai with Jagdish Mama at seven, college by nine, Thursday sessions with a trained therapist at the clinic above the chemist. At a cousin's wedding the week before, an aunt had leaned in. "Tell us everything, what exactly happened?" Pooja smiled. "I'm safe now. That's the part I want to talk about." Jagdish Mama had quietly steered the aunt toward the sweets. Today the junction slid past. Pooja noticed she had been thinking about her exam, not the crash. She still remembered it. It just didn't grab her by the throat anymore.

qa.q: When does Pooja see the trained therapist?
qa.a: She has Thursday sessions with a trained therapist at the clinic above the chemist.

qa.q: Why did Pooja answer the aunt with "I'm safe now" instead of telling the whole story?
qa.a: She felt uneasy retelling the crash on demand, and wanted to keep control over what she shared, so she chose the part she was comfortable with.

qa.q: What choice did Pooja make at the junction this time, and why did it help?
qa.a: She counted the flower stalls instead of bracing in fear, which kept her mind in the present until the junction passed.

qa.q: How might Jagdish Mama see Pooja's healing when he steers the aunt away?
qa.a: He seems to understand that she is recovering at her own pace, and wants to protect her right to share only what feels right.

grounding: It shows a young adult recovering from a crash through safety, steady routines, a trained therapist and choosing what to share, with the memory losing its hold.

passage:
Monsoon rain drummed on the hostel window. Gargi, Shreya's roommate, lowered her voice.
"Is the rain bad for you?"
"You don't have to whisper, Gargi. I can talk about the flood. Some of it."
"Sorry. My aunt knows a yoga teacher who does 'trauma healing'. Want the number?"
"Thanks, but I've booked the campus counselling centre. I checked, the counsellor there is trained for this."
"And the five a.m. alarm every day? Is that part of it?"
"Walk, bath, lecture notes. Same order, every day. When it rains, the order holds me."
"Do you want to tell me what happened that night?"
"Not tonight. Maybe never all of it. Is that okay?"
"Of course it is. Chai?"
"Yes. And Gargi? I don't think I'll ever forget the water in our stairwell. I just want to hear rain and not jump up."
The drizzle thickened. Shreya stayed on her bed, both hands around her cup.

qa.q: What does Shreya do every day after the five a.m. alarm?
qa.a: Walk, bath, lecture notes, in the same order, every day.

qa.q: How does Shreya feel when Gargi asks about that night, and what shows it?
qa.a: Shreya still feels it is too painful to retell; she says "Not tonight. Maybe never all of it" and checks whether that is okay.

qa.q: Which choice did Shreya make about getting help, and why was it sound?
qa.a: She booked the campus counselling centre after checking the counsellor was trained, instead of taking an untrained healer's number.

qa.q: What is it like for Gargi to hear "Not tonight"?
qa.a: Gargi may feel unsure how to help, but by simply offering chai she learns that support can mean respecting Shreya's limits.

grounding: It shows a young adult after a flood keeping a steady routine, choosing a trained counsellor, sharing only what feels right and hoping for the past to loosen its hold.

subtype: Sadness after a loss in children [Actor]
passage: Two days after Dadi's funeral, Ritu sat by the buffalo shed and cried into her frock until her nose ran. An hour later she was hopping across chalk squares in the lane with Ayesha from next door, shrieking with laughter when Ayesha wobbled. At dusk, while Papa lit the lamp, Ritu asked, "When is Dadi coming back from the hospital?" It was the third time that day. Papa put the matchbox down. "Dadi died, Ritu. Her body stopped working, and she can't come back. We all miss her." Ritu nodded. Then she asked if she could still feed the buffalo in the morning, the way Dadi used to. "Yes," said Papa. "Six o'clock, same as always."

qa.q: What did Ritu ask Papa at dusk?
qa.a: When is Dadi coming back from the hospital?

qa.q: Why might Ritu keep asking the same question about Dadi?
qa.a: She is confused and still hoping; the idea that Dadi can never come back is hard for her to hold, so she checks again.

qa.q: What choice did Papa make when Ritu asked a third time, and why did it help?
qa.a: He stopped, gave the same honest, simple answer and kept the six o'clock routine, giving her both the truth and something steady.

qa.q: What might Ayesha think when Ritu laughs so soon after the funeral?

passage: On Sunday mornings in Toronto, Rania used to video-call Jiddo while Mum made pancakes. This Sunday the laptop stayed shut. Rania ate two pancakes, built a blanket fort with her little brother and laughed so hard she snorted. Then she saw Jiddo's old scarf on the hook and sobbed on the hallway floor. Her mother, Fatima, sat down beside her. After a while Rania whispered, "Did Jiddo die because I didn't call last week?" "No, habibti. Jiddo was very old and very sick. Nothing you did or didn't do made him die." At bedtime Rania asked again. Fatima gave the same answer, in the same gentle words. "Can we still have pancakes on Sundays?" "Every Sunday."

qa.q: What did Rania see that made her sob?
qa.a: Jiddo's old scarf on the hook.

qa.q: What was Rania worried about when she whispered to her mother?
qa.a: She was afraid that Jiddo died because she didn't call last week, so she felt it might be her fault.

qa.q: Which choice by Fatima at bedtime helped Rania, and why?
qa.a: Fatima answered the repeated question again with the same simple, honest words, without impatience, so Rania heard clearly that it was not her fault.

qa.q: How might Rania's little brother see her laughing in the fort and then crying soon after?
qa.a: He may be puzzled, but it shows that a grieving child can play happily one moment and cry the next; both are normal.

grounding: It shows a child abroad grieving Jiddo in waves of play and tears, repeating a question and needing honest words and the Sunday routine.

passage:
Dear Ritu Didi,
Thank you for the photo of Nana at your wedding. I've stuck it inside my maths notebook.
It's been three months. Some days I'm fine, and then a song on the bus hits me like a wave. I get angry too: at the hospital, at Nana for not telling us he felt ill, at myself for skipping his birthday call to finish a game.
Yesterday Isha showed me a silly video in the library and I laughed out loud. Then I felt terrible, as if laughing meant I'd forgotten him.
Mum says laughing is allowed. We talk about Nana every Sunday over his favourite jalebi.
You asked me to tell you if the sad feeling spreads to everything. Right now it's mostly about Nana. I still like drawing and my friends. If that changes, I'll tell Mum and the school counsellor. Promise.
Love,
Nikita

qa.q: Where did Nikita stick the photo of Nana?
qa.a: Inside Nikita's maths notebook.

qa.q: Why did Nikita feel terrible after laughing in the library?
qa.a: Nikita felt ashamed, as if laughing meant Nana had been forgotten.

qa.q: What choice has Nikita made in case the sadness spreads, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Nikita has promised to tell Mum and the school counsellor if the sadness spreads to everything, so help would come early.

qa.q: How might Ritu Didi feel reading that the sadness is still mostly about Nana?
qa.a: She may feel relieved that Nikita still enjoys drawing and friends, while staying ready to help if that changes.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose grief for a grandparent brings sadness, anger, guilt and ashamed laughter, still tied to the loss and eased by family support.

passage: People think the year after someone dies is just sad. For me it was messy. I'm Vandana, and Jagdish Sir coached our kabaddi team from the time I was eleven. When he died in the bus accident, I was angry first, at the driver, at the rain, at myself for sulking through our last practice instead of saying thanks. Then in our first match without him, I made a raid, the whole team screamed, and I laughed. On the ride home I felt sick with shame, like I'd betrayed him. For a while it was only about him, and I could carry that. But around March I stopped caring about anything, even drawing, and I kept thinking I was useless. My mum noticed I'd stopped eating with the family and booked a counsellor that same week. That helped a lot. Now when I laugh on the mat, I think he'd have laughed too.

qa.q: Which sport did Jagdish Sir coach?
qa.a: Kabaddi.

qa.q: Why did Vandana feel sick with shame on the ride home?
qa.a: Vandana had laughed after a raid in the first match without Jagdish Sir and felt that the laughter betrayed him.

qa.q: What was the turning point around March, and why did it matter?
qa.a: When Vandana stopped caring about anything and felt useless, Mum noticed and booked a counsellor that same week, getting help before things got worse.

qa.q: How might Vandana's mum have seen the change around March?
qa.a: She likely saw that it was no longer only grief for Jagdish Sir but a sadness spreading into everything, so she acted quickly.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose grief for a coach mixes anger, guilt and ashamed laughter, and whose family seeks help when the sadness spreads to everything.

passage: I'm Gurleen, and my roommate Mridul lost his father in June. By November I had stopped telling myself it was only grief. Mridul hadn't been to a lecture in weeks, slept through the afternoons and left plates untouched on the desk we shared. What frightened me most was one night when he said, flatly, "Everyone would be better off without me." I sat down on his bed. My heart was hammering, but I asked him straight out whether he was thinking of not living. He said, "Sometimes." I told him I was glad he'd told me and that I wasn't leaving the room. We called the campus crisis line together, and the next morning I walked with him to the counsellor. She said grief and depression can arrive together, and that getting help wasn't a betrayal of his dad. He still misses his father. But he's getting help now, and he's back in class.

qa.q: When did Mridul's father die?
qa.a: In June.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel when asking Mridul the direct question, and what shows it?
qa.a: Gurleen was frightened; Gurleen's heart was hammering, yet the question was still asked plainly.

qa.q: What choice did Gurleen make after Mridul said "Sometimes", and why was it right?
qa.a: Gurleen stayed in the room, called the campus crisis line with Mridul and walked him to the counsellor next morning, so he was not alone and got professional help.

qa.q: How might Mridul have felt when Gurleen asked him straight out?
qa.a: He may have felt some relief at being asked plainly, which made it easier for him to admit how bad things were.

grounding: It shows a roommate noticing, months after a death, that grief has turned into not functioning and talk of not wanting to live, and encouraging professional help.

passage:
Supervisor's note, bakery kitchen, 14 February. Written by Rashmi.
Uday's mother died last June. For months he worked through it quietly, and I let him keep her photo in the locker room. Lately it is different. He has come in late nine times this month, forgot the ovens twice and stands staring at the dough. Today he said, "I'm useless at everything now. It won't ever get better." That sounded bigger than missing her.
What I did next: I took him to the back office and said I was worried about him, not about the bread. I asked plainly whether he had thoughts of ending his life. He said no, only that everything feels heavy. I told him grief and low mood can come together, and that a doctor or counsellor could help. We looked up the free counselling clinic near the station together, and he booked for Friday. I gave him that morning off.

qa.q: How many times has Uday come in late this month?
qa.a: Nine times.

qa.q: Why was Rashmi worried that Uday's words were bigger than missing his mother?
qa.a: Rashmi felt alarmed because he called himself useless at everything and said it won't ever get better, which sounded like hopelessness beyond the loss.

qa.q: Which step by Rashmi turned worry into action?
qa.a: Rashmi asked plainly about thoughts of ending his life, then looked up the free counselling clinic with Uday so he could book a visit, with that morning off.

qa.q: What might it be like for Uday to hear that Rashmi was worried about him, not the bread?
qa.a: He may feel seen as a person rather than a failing worker, which makes accepting help easier.

grounding: It shows a supervisor noticing that months after a loss a young worker cannot function and feels worthless, and encouraging professional help.

passage:
12 March, night
Went to Sharmila's home today for the thirteenth-day prayers for her father. I'd never been to one. Cousins were rolling puris in the courtyard, someone had put his reading glasses beside the photo, and everyone ate together on long mats. It felt like the whole lane was holding the family up.
But I also heard an aunt tell Sharmila, "Be strong, beta, don't cry in front of the guests." Sharmila nodded and went completely still after that, as if she'd left the room without moving.
Later an old neighbour sat with her and asked, "What was he like on Sunday mornings?" Sharmila laughed, then cried, then told us about his terrible puns. Nobody rushed her.
I'm her colleague, not family, and I don't know the right words. But tomorrow I'll send her one of his puns and ask how she's doing.
Ayesha

qa.q: What had someone put beside the photo?
qa.a: His reading glasses.

qa.q: What does Sharmila going completely still suggest about how she felt after the aunt spoke?
qa.a: It suggests she felt she had to hide her grief and pulled into herself, alone even in a full house.

qa.q: What did Ayesha decide to do tomorrow, and why is it a good choice?
qa.a: To send Sharmila one of her father's puns and ask how she is, which invites her to speak of him without being hurried.

qa.q: How did the neighbour's question change things for Sharmila?
qa.a: Being asked what her father was like let her laugh, cry and share his puns, so she felt accompanied instead of told to be strong.

grounding: It shows a colleague at thirteenth-day prayers seeing shared meals hold a family up, and noticing that being told to be strong silences the mourner while gentle questions help.

passage:
Jahnavi: How was today? Thinking of you.
Zeenat: Full house. Neighbours have sent food every day since Nani passed. Nobody has cooked in our kitchen for a week.
Jahnavi: That sounds like a lot of people holding you all.
Zeenat: It is. The prayer gathering was nice. Everyone shared one memory of her.
Zeenat: But Chachu keeps saying "Be strong, you're the eldest grandchild." So I cry in the bathroom.
Jahnavi: You don't have to be strong with me.
Jahnavi: What memory did you share?
Zeenat: That she cheated at ludo and denied it every single time.
Zeenat: Sorry, long message coming.
Jahnavi: Take your time. I'm not going anywhere.
Jahnavi read the last line twice, put the kettle on and kept the chat open on her lap.

qa.q: Since when have neighbours sent food?
qa.a: Every day since Nani passed.

passage:
Subject: Can I meet you this week?
Dear Noor Ma'am,
I'm Manoj from 10C. You said in assembly that we could write to you if something was taking over our days. I think this is.
I keep scrolling through photos of people with perfect arms and flat stomachs. I know most of them are filtered, but I still compare myself. I've covered the mirror in my room with a poster. Last Sunday I pretended to have a stomach-ache so I wouldn't have to go to my cousin's engagement, because everyone takes photos. In class I'm thinking about how I look instead of the lesson. It feels like if I looked different I'd matter more.
My friends say everyone feels like this sometimes. Maybe. But for me it's all day now.
Could I come and see you after lunch on Wednesday?
Manoj

qa.a: A poster.

passage: Thanks for having me on the youth show, Urmila. So, last year I quit swimming. Not because I stopped loving it. Because of the changing room. I'd spent nights comparing myself to people online, all shiny and edited, and in my head I was the wrong shape. I stopped going to family dinners because someone always says, "You've grown." I'd take three selfies, edit my face, and still hate them. It got to where every thought was about my body: in maths, at the bus stop, before sleep. One day Coach asked why I'd stopped coming, and I just said it. He didn't laugh. He said lots of people feel this way, but if it's filling the whole day, a doctor or counsellor should know. My mum took me that week. I'm Abhinav, by the way, and I'm back in the pool now. Some days.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav quit swimming?
qa.a: Because of the changing room.

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel about the selfies even after editing them?
qa.a: Abhinav still hated them, which shows a harsh view of Abhinav's own body that no editing could fix.

qa.q: What choice changed things for Abhinav, and what followed?
qa.a: Abhinav told Coach the real reason; Coach said a doctor or counsellor should know, and Mum took Abhinav that week.

qa.q: How might Coach have seen Abhinav's absence before that day?
qa.a: He may have thought Abhinav had lost interest, and learned only by asking that a painful body worry was keeping Abhinav away.

grounding: It shows a teenager comparing their body to edited images, avoiding the pool and family dinners, and getting help once the thoughts filled every part of the day.

passage:
Zainab,
I'm writing this because saying it in the canteen felt wrong.
For about a month you've told me you already ate at home, but your tiffin comes back full, and you've started eating alone in the library. Every time we meet you ask which clothes make you look smaller, and you talk about shape more than about cricket, which you used to love.
I'm not going to say anything about how you look. That isn't the point. The point is that I miss you and I'm worried.
I won't nag you to eat either. But I think a doctor should know what's going on. Would you talk to your Ammi, or come with me to the school nurse on Monday? I'll wait outside.
You can be angry with me. I'm still your friend.
Abhinav

qa.q: Where has Zainab started eating?
qa.a: Alone in the library.

qa.q: What is Abhinav worried about, and what shows it?

qa.a: Abhinav chose not to comment on Zainab's looks or nag about eating, and instead offered to go with Zainab to the school nurse.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel reading "You can be angry with me. I'm still your friend"?

passage: When the group leader asked me to share tonight, I almost said no. I'm Binita, Jaya's mother. Last winter Jaya, who is fifteen, started saying she'd eaten at a friend's house. Then I found her lunch wrapped in paper at the bottom of her schoolbag. She began taking her plate to her room. And every conversation turned to her waist, her arms, who looked thin. My first move was wrong. I put a full plate in front of her and said, "You'll sit until it's finished." She cried and locked her door. That night I knocked and said only, "I love you. I'm not angry. I'm scared, and I think we need the doctor's help." I didn't say one word about her body. Next morning we went to our family doctor together, and he sent us to a specialist. It's slow. But she talks to me again.

qa.q: Where did Binita find Jaya's lunch?
qa.a: Wrapped in paper at the bottom of her schoolbag.

qa.q: How did Jaya likely feel when told to sit until the plate was finished?

passage: Exam week, and a power cut had shut the hostel mess early. Baljeet didn't mind. For months she had kept private rules: no food until every chapter was revised, only the same plain things, never in front of anyone. When her marks slipped or her father's calls turned sharp, the rules felt like the one thing she could control. Skipping felt clean, almost calm, for an hour. Then, on the stairs before the chemistry paper, the walls tilted and she sat down hard. Afreen from the next room crouched beside her. "This isn't the first time, is it?" Baljeet shook her head. After the paper, Afreen walked her to the campus health centre. Baljeet had planned to say "just tired". Instead she told the doctor about the rules. The doctor listened without scolding and referred her to a specialist.

qa.a: No food until every chapter was revised.

passage: After the team lead snapped at her in front of everyone, Dilnaz took the lift down to the office basement with a plastic bag of snacks bought on her break. She ate fast on the stairwell, without tasting anything. For ten minutes the noise in her head went quiet. Then came the heavy stomach, the shame, the wrappers pushed deep into the dustbin under other rubbish so nobody would see. It had happened four evenings this week. Back at the flat she told Damini, her flatmate, that she wasn't hungry, and skipped dinner, the way she always did afterwards. That night Damini found her awake at two. Dilnaz meant to say nothing. Instead she said, "I think I'm using food to get through the day, and it's hurting me." Damini didn't laugh or lecture. She held out her phone. "Let's book the doctor for Saturday. I'll come with you."

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz push the wrappers?
qa.a: Deep into the dustbin under other rubbish.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz feel during the ten minutes of eating, and afterwards?
qa.a: A brief quiet relief while eating, then a heavy stomach and shame.

qa.q: Which choice at two in the morning changed things?

passage:
Dear Yamini Bua,
I wanted to thank you for Sunday lunch.
Since I was twelve, the family has had a nickname for me that I won't write here. This year, after a term of hostel food and football, everyone suddenly said, "Wah, so slim now, finally handsome!" I know they meant it kindly. But I realised the praise and the teasing were the same thing: both about my body, both telling me that's what counts. Now I feel every eye on my plate. If I take a second roti, I wait for someone to say something.
When Chachi started on my waist again, you said, "Vishal, you've been playing so much football, are you sleeping enough?" The whole table moved on to exams.
Could you keep doing that? I think the others listen to you.
With love,
Vishal

qa.q: What did Yamini Bua ask Vishal at Sunday lunch?
qa.a: "Vishal, you've been playing so much football, are you sleeping enough?"

qa.q: What does Vishal worry about when taking a second roti?

qa.q: Which choice by Yamini Bua shifted the table, and why did it work?
qa.a: Yamini Bua turned the talk from Vishal's waist to football and sleep, focusing on health rather than looks, so the table moved on.

grounding: It shows a young adult who, teased and then praised for their body, learns that looks are what count and feels watched at meals, until talk about health shifts the mood.

passage: People think compliments can't hurt. I'm Preeti, and I'm speaking at this wellness evening because of our college canteen. At school they called me names for being tall and bony. Then in college the same body got praise: "You should model." "Don't ever gain weight." Different words, same message: my body was the most interesting thing about me. I started to feel eyes on me at every meal. If I ate a samosa, someone said, "Careful!" If I skipped one, someone said, "Wow, discipline." So I stopped eating in the canteen at all. My roommate Pooja noticed. She didn't make a speech. One day she just said at our table, "New rule: no body talk while we eat. Tell me about your day instead." People laughed, and then they actually did it. It sounds small. It let me eat lunch again.

qa.q: What was Pooja's new rule at the table?
qa.a: No body talk while we eat.

qa.q: Why did Preeti feel watched at every meal?
qa.a: Both eating and skipping food drew comments, so Preeti felt judged over every food choice.

qa.q: What made Pooja's choice at the table effective?
qa.a: It was simple and friendly, swapping body talk for "Tell me about your day", so people could change the habit without feeling scolded.

qa.q: How might the people who said "You should model" see their own words?
qa.a: They probably thought they were giving compliments, not realising the praise taught Preeti that looks were Preeti's value.

grounding: It shows how teasing and praise about a body both teach that appearance is value and make meals feel watched, and how a roommate's kind table rule changes the climate.

passage: The bus to the district town rattled past mustard fields, and Alka's cousin Rekha held up her phone. "Selfie? Wait, let me put the slimming filter." Alka covered the screen, laughing. "No filter. My face came all this way, it can be in the photo." A year ago Alka would have deleted every picture of herself. She had skipped meals, checked her reflection in every shop window and called herself ugly under her breath. When it got bad enough that she fainted at the tailoring shop, her mother took her to the doctor, and now she saw a counsellor in town every other Saturday. That was where they were going. At the bus stand Alka bought two plates of poha. "Lunch first. Always lunch first." Rekha frowned at her own face in the bus window. "I look huge today." "You look like someone who climbed to the hilltop temple faster than me this morning," Alka said.

qa.q: What did Alka buy at the bus stand?
qa.a: Two plates of poha.

qa.q: What does Alka's laughing "No filter" suggest about how she now feels about her face?
qa.a: It suggests she feels comfortable being seen as she is, unlike a year ago when she deleted every picture of herself.

qa.q: What turning point led Alka to a counsellor?
qa.a: When she fainted at the tailoring shop, her mother took her to the doctor, which led to regular counselling in town.

qa.q: How might Rekha feel hearing Alka's reply about the hilltop temple?
qa.a: Rekha may feel surprised and a little lighter, hearing her body praised for what it did instead of judged for how it looks.

grounding: It shows a young woman in a small town refusing filters, eating regular meals, speaking kindly about bodies and keeping up counselling after a serious struggle.
